description: Kṛṣṇa knows all of his many past births and those of Arjuna, while Arjuna does not know them (4.5).

The one unattached to external contacts finds the happiness that is in the self and enjoys imperishable happiness (5.21); the yogin whose happiness, delight and light are within (antaḥ-sukha, antar-ārāma, antar-jyotis) becomes Brahman and attains brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24).
The simile for the controlled mind of the yogin practising the yoga of the self: a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker (6.19).

The state called yoga: the mind, restrained by practice, comes to rest; seeing the self by the self one is content in the self; one knows boundless happiness grasped by the intellect and beyond the senses; one does not waver from reality, counts no gain greater, and is not shaken even by heavy sorrow; it is the unyoking from union with sorrow (6.20–23).

Supreme happiness comes to the yogin whose mind is at peace, whose rajas is stilled, who has become Brahman and is stainless (6.27); constantly yoking himself he easily enjoys the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman (6.28).

By knowledge one sees all beings in the self and then in the Lord (4.35); the yogin yoked in yoga, seeing the same everywhere, sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self (6.29); whoever sees the Lord everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him (6.30); established in oneness he worships the Lord as abiding in all beings (6.31).

Arjuna's difficulty: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to hold as the wind, so the yoga of sameness does not seem able to stand steady (6.33–34); Kṛṣṇa grants this and names practice and dispassion as the means (6.35).

stage: yogabhraṣṭa (one fallen from yoga), in a new birth
description: Reborn among the pure or among yogins, the one fallen from yoga regains the connection with understanding of his former body and strives again; he is carried along by his former practice even without his will (6.43–44).
